source_text: υἱὸς ἢ τὸ πνεῦμα. οὔτε γὰρ ἂν ὁ ὑπέρτατος καὶ πλούσιος ἐν ἐλέει παρὰ τοῦ χείρονος 71 καὶ πενεστέρου ἐδανείσατο, οὔτε ἡμεῖς διττῶς καὶ ἀνομοίως ἐνηργήμεθα. καὶ μέντοι ποῖον ἔχει λόγον, ἄνθρωπον μὲν καλῶν, φέρε εἰπεῖν, ἢ κακῶν εἶναι ποιητὴν καὶ δημιουργόν, τὸ δὲ πνεῦμα μὴ εἶναι τοῦτο; ἀλλ' ὁ ἄνθρωπος κατὰ συγχώρησιν μὲν τοῦ θεοῦ πράττει τοῦτο ἢ ἐκεῖνο· ἀπὸ οὐσίας δὲ τῆς ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ προοισθείσης, ἄψυχον δημιουργεῖ, ὁ δ' ἂν θέλοι, οὐ μὴν καὶ οὐσίαν αὐτήν, ὡς ἔφαμεν ἤδη. τὸ δέ γε πνεῦμα καὶ αὐθεντικῶς ποιεῖ, καὶ οὐσίαν ἐκ μὴ ὄντων ὑφίστησιν, ἅτε συνεργὸν καὶ πνοὴ παντοκράτορος. διόπερ ὁ θεὸς ἐν τῷ Ἰεζεκιήλ, τὸ μὲν ἡμέτερον πνεῦμα ἀνακαινίζεσθαι, τὸ δὲ ἅγιον πνεῦμα ἀνακαινίζειν, καὶ οὐχ ἁπλῶς πνεῦμα εἶναι, ἀλλ' ἑαυτοῦ κυρίως ὑποδεικνύς, τοιάδε θεσπίζει· «καὶ δώσω ὑμῖν καρδίαν καινήν, καὶ πνεῦμα καινὸν δώσω ὑμῖν· καὶ ἀφε λῶ τὴν καρδίαν τὴν λιθίνην ἐκ τῆς σαρκὸς ὑμῶν, καὶ δώσω ὑμῖν καρδίαν σαρκίνην, καὶ τὸ πνεῦμα μου δώσω ἐν ὑμῖν.» οἱ δὲ καὶ τῶν θείων φωνῶν τούτων ὀλιγωροῦντες, καὶ ἐν ἀπορίᾳ πάσῃ τῶν δικαίων καθεστῶτες, λοιπὸν ταῖς ἔξωθεν τέχναις ἀποκέχρηνται, καὶ ἐπ' ἄλλα καὶ ἄλλα μεταφέρειν ἐπιχειροῦσιν τὰ οὕτως σαφῶς εἰρημένα. φάσκουσι γὰρ λέξεσιν αὐταῖς· νεκροὺς ὁ δημιουργήσας, τοὺς νεκρουμένους ἐγείρει μόνος. ἀρχιτέκτονος γὰρ ἔργον φθειρόμενον ζωγράφος οὐκ ἂν διορθώσαιτο, ἀλλ' οὐδὲ ναυπηγοῦ θηρευτής, ἀλλ' οὐδέ γε οἰκοδόμου δρομεύς· ἀλλὰ γὰρ ἀρχιτέκτονος ἀρχιτέκτων καὶ ναυπηγοῦ ναυπηγός. τὸ δὲ ἅγιον πνεῦμα, φησίν, οὔτε νεκροὺς ἤγειρεν, οὔτε ἐδημιούργησεν· ἅπαξ γάρ, φησίν, ἐπὶ τοῦ Ἀδὰμ δεδημιούργηται ἡ ἀνθρώπων φύσις· καὶ οὔτε ἑτέρα παρ' ἐκείνην, οὔτε πολλάκις. ἀλλὰ καὶ ἡ Εὔα συνεκτίσθη μὲν τῷ Ἀδὰμ τῷ κοινῷ τῆς φύσεως λόγῳ, μετὰ ταῦτα δὲ διεμορφώθη. ἡμεῖς δὲ οἱ ὀρθόδοξοι, ἐπειδὴ μάλιστα θεϊκῆς δυνάμεως γνώρισμα τὸ δημιουργῆσαι καὶ νεκροὺς ἐγεῖραι, ὁμολογοῦμεν τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα ταῦτα πεποιηκὸς εἶναι θεόν· «τῷ λόγῳ» γὰρ «κυρίου οἱ οὐρανοὶ ἐστερεώθησαν, καὶ τῷ πνεύματι τοῦ στόματος αὐτοῦ πᾶσαι αἱ δυνάμεις αὐτῶν,» καὶ ἐπειδὴ ἀρχῆθεν, δημιουργουμένων πάντων, συμπαρῆν καὶ ἀχωρίστως εἶχεν τῇ θεότητι καὶ τῇ ἐνεργείᾳ, διὰ τοῦτο καὶ ἀνακαινιζομένων αὐτῶν συμπάρεστι καὶ συμμνημονεύεται. ὅπερ γὰρ εἰρήκασιν αὐτοὶ οὗτοι, οὐκ ἦν ἑτέρας οὐσίας ὅ ἐστιν φύσεως τὸ ἀνακαινίσαι, εἰ μὴ τῆς τοῦ κτίσαντος. περὶ οὖν τῶν ὄντων καὶ πολιτευομένων ὡς μὴ ὄντων, ἀλλὰ νῦν πνευματικῶς καὶ θειοτέρως κτιζομένων ὁ ∆αυὶδ καὶ ὁ Παῦλος κηρύσσει, ὡς προελέχθη καὶ ὡς πολλαχοῦ εὑρήσομεν. ἐπιλείψει με γὰρ ἂν ὁ πᾶς χρόνος, εἰ πάντων πανταχοῦ μνημονεύειν ἐθελήσω. εἰ μὴ οὖν ἑτέρως μὲν ταῖς γραφαῖς, ἑτέρως δὲ αὐτοῖς ἐκείνοις ἐδόκει, πρῶτον μὲν οὖν κἄν ποτε παρενεθυμήθησαν τὰ θεῖα γραφεῖα τὰ ἐν τῷ βιβλίῳ τῷδε καὶ τῷ πρὸ αὐτοῦ μνημονευθέντα· τί γὰρ ἄν, ἀκούοντες ταῦτα, φήσαιεν τὸν χρήσαντα αὐτὰ διδάσκειν; δεύτερον δὲ ἐλογίσαντο ἄν, ὅτιπερ, ὃν τρόπον τοῦ υἱοῦ κτίσαντος συμποιητὴς ὁ πατήρ ἐστιν τῇ εὐδοκήσει, οὕτω καὶ τὸ πνεῦμα αὐτοῦ· καὶ οὐκ εἰς τὴν τῶν οὐχ ὁμοίων ἐξέτασιν τῶν συνάρσεως τῆς ἀλλήλων καὶ τῆς ἀπὸ τοῦ χρόνου δεομένων καὶ μηδὲ πληρούντων ἑτοίμως καὶ πανταχόθεν ἀμέμπτως τὴν ἐνθύμησιν τὰ τῆς ἀμίκτου ἅπασιν μακαρίας τριάδος τῆς καὶ ἡμᾶς ἀποτελεσάσης, δημιουργοὺς λόγων τε καὶ ὑλῶν ἐπισκευῆς, ἤγαγον, λέγοντες, ἅπερ μήποτ' ἔφασαν. τί γὰρ ἢ ὡς πηλίκοι εἴποιμεν τῷ ἅπαξ θελήσαντι θεῷ πατρὶ διὰ τοῦ υἱοῦ λόγου πάντα ὑποστῆναι; ἀμέλει τοι περὶ τοῦ ἐκ σπέρματος ∆αυὶδ καὶ Ἀβραὰμ καὶ ἐκ ῥίζης Ἰεσσαὶ κατὰ σάρκα κεκήρυκται, ὡς ἀρτίως εἴρηται· «τὸ γὰρ ἐν αὐτῇ γεννηθὲν ἐκ πνεύματός ἐστιν ἁγίου,» ἵνα κἀντεῦθεν ὁμόλογον ᾖ, ὡς συνεργὸν ἦν τῷ ἀγαθουργῷ δημιουργῷ τὸ ἁγιαστικὸν πνεῦμα. διὸ καὶ αὖθις γέγραπται· «ἤγετο ὁ Ἰησοῦς ἐν πνεύματι ἐπὶ τὴν ἔρημον·» ἐπειδὴ συνῆν αὐτῷ τὸ ἡγεμονικὸν πνεῦμα, ὡς θεὸς θεῷ καὶ ὡς πάντα συνέχων καὶ πανταχοῦ παρὼν τῷ, ἐφ' ὃν πάντα ἐστήρικται, καὶ ἐν πᾶσιν ὄντι καὶ πληροῦντι τὰ πάντα. ἐπεὶ μή γε τῷ ἐκείνων λόγῳ καὶ τῷ τρόπῳ οὔτε ὁ πατὴρ 72 δημιουργὸς ἢ νεκροὺς ἐγείρων. πάντα γὰρ διὰ τοῦ υἱοῦ ἐγένετο ἀπόνως. πόνος γὰρ πάθος ἐστί· πάθος δὲ ὁδὸς ἐπὶ φθοράν. οὐκ ἀρνούμενοι δὲ τὸν δεσπότην σεσαρκῶσθαι δίχα ἁμαρτίας ἐκ τῆς φύσεως τοῦ Ἀδάμ, ὅ ἐστιν ἐκ τῆς παρθένου, ἢ τῆς ἡμετέρας ταῦτά φαμεν, μᾶλλον δὲ καὶ βεβαιοῦμεν τοῦτο διὰ τοῦ λέγειν ἐκ
pass_a_gloss: [Continuing from the previous section: ... in no respect will be unlike the] Son or the Spirit. For neither would the highest and rich in mercy have borrowed from the worse [page number 71, debris] and poorer, nor would we have been worked upon doubly and unequally. And indeed what reason does it have, that man is maker and craftsman of good things, let us say, or of bad, but the Spirit is not this? But man does this or that by permission of God; and from a substance brought forward beforehand by God he crafts, lifeless, whatever he might wish, but not the substance itself, as we already said. But the Spirit both makes with authority, and gives subsistence to substance out of things that are not, inasmuch as fellow-worker and breath of the Almighty. Wherefore God in Ezekiel, showing that our spirit is renewed, but the Holy Spirit renews, and that it is not simply a spirit but properly his own, decrees such things: 'and I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will give you; and I will take away [the word split across a line] the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a fleshly heart, and my Spirit I will give in you.' But they, belittling even these divine utterances, and being in every perplexity of just [arguments], have at last made use of the outside arts, and attempt to transfer onto other and other things the things so clearly said. For they say in the very words: the one who created [them] alone raises the dead, those being put to death. For a painter would not set right the decaying work of a master builder, nor a hunter [that] of a shipwright, nor indeed a runner [that] of a house-builder; but a master builder [that] of a master builder and a shipwright [that] of a shipwright. But the Holy Spirit, he says, neither raised dead nor created; for once, he says, in the case of Adam the nature of men has been created; and neither another besides that one, nor many times. But even Eve was created together with Adam by the common principle of the nature, and after these things was formed. But we the orthodox, since the mark of divine power above all is to create and to raise the dead, confess the Holy Spirit, having done these things, to be God: for 'by the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their powers', and since from the beginning, all things being created, it was present together and was inseparably [joined] in the Godhead and the working, because of this also, they being renewed, it is present together and is mentioned together. For what these very men have said: to renew was not of another essence, that is nature, except of that of the one who created. About those, then, who are and conduct life as not being, but now are being created spiritually and more divinely, David and Paul preach, as was said before and as we shall find in many places. For all the time would fail me if I should wish to mention all things everywhere. If then it did not seem one way to the Scriptures and another way to those very men, first then they would at some time have taken to heart the divine writings mentioned in this book and in the one before it; for what would they, hearing these things, say that the one who gave them as oracles teaches? And second they would have reckoned that, in the way in which, the Son creating, the Father is co-maker by his good pleasure, so also his Spirit; and they would not have brought the things of the blessed Trinity, unmixed with all things, which also completed us, craftsmen of words and of the working-up of materials, into the examination of things not alike, needing the joint help of one another and that from time, and not fulfilling readily and blamelessly on every side the intention, saying things which would they had never said. For what or as how great [beings] would we say to God the Father, who once willed that all things come into being through the Son, the Word? Certainly about the one from the seed of David and Abraham and from the root of Jesse according to flesh it has been proclaimed, as was just said: 'for what was begotten in her is from Holy Spirit', that from here too it may be agreed that the sanctifying Spirit was fellow-worker with the good-working Creator. Wherefore also again it has been written: 'Jesus was led in the Spirit into the wilderness', since the guiding Spirit was with him, as God with God, and as holding all things together and present everywhere, with the one on whom all things have been founded, and being in all and filling all things. Since surely not: by their reasoning and manner neither the Father [page number 72, debris] [is] creator or raising the dead. For all things came to be through the Son without toil. For toil is a passion; and passion a road to corruption. And not denying that the Master was made flesh without sin from the nature of Adam, that is from the virgin, or ours, we say these things, but rather we even confirm this by saying 'from' [continues in the next section] ...
pass_b_english: …Son or the Spirit. For neither would the Most High, who is rich in mercy (Ephesians 2:4), have borrowed from one inferior and poorer, nor would we have been worked upon in two ways, and unequally. And indeed, what sense does it make that a man should be the maker and craftsman of good things, say, or of bad, while the Spirit is not? A man does this or that by God’s permission; and out of a substance that God has supplied beforehand he fashions whatever lifeless thing he may wish, but not the substance itself, as we have already said. The Spirit, however, makes with sovereign authority, and brings substance into being out of things that are not, as fellow-worker and “breath of the Almighty” (Job 33:4).

This is why God in Ezekiel, showing that our spirit is renewed while the Holy Spirit renews, and that this is not simply a spirit but properly his own, declares: “And I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will give you; I will take away the heart of stone out of your flesh and give you a heart of flesh; and my Spirit I will put in you” (Ezekiel 36:26-27).

But these men, making light even of these divine words and finding themselves at a complete loss for just arguments, have at last resorted to the arts of outsiders, and try to shift onto this thing and that what has been said so clearly. For they say, in these very words: “The dead, those who are put to death, are raised only by him who created them. A painter would not repair a master builder’s work when it decays, nor would a hunter repair a shipwright’s, nor a runner a house-builder’s; no, a master builder repairs a master builder’s work, and a shipwright a shipwright’s. But the Holy Spirit,” he says, “neither raised the dead nor created. For human nature,” he says, “was created once, in Adam; no other has been created besides it, nor has it been created many times. Even Eve was created together with Adam by the common principle of nature, and was given her own form afterwards.”

But we who are orthodox, since creating and raising the dead are above all the mark of divine power, confess that the Holy Spirit, who has done these things, is God. For “by the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their powers” (Psalm 33:6). And since from the beginning, when all things were being created, he was present with God and was inseparable from him in Godhead and in working, for that reason he is also present with him and named with him when they are being renewed. For, as these very men have said, to renew belonged to no other essence, that is, nature, than that of the one who created. So it is of those who exist and live as though they did not exist, but are now being created spiritually and in a more divine way, that David and Paul preach, as was said before and as we shall find in many places. Indeed, all my time would fail me if I chose to mention every passage everywhere.

If, then, it had not seemed one thing to the Scriptures and another to these men, then first, they would at some point have taken to heart the divine writings recalled in this book and in the one before it. For what would they say, when they heard them, that the one who uttered these oracles teaches? Second, they would have reasoned that, just as the Father is co-maker by his good pleasure when the Son creates, so too is his Spirit. And they would not have dragged the things of the blessed Trinity, which mingles with nothing and which made us too, craftsmen of words and of the shaping of materials, into comparison with things unlike it: things that need one another’s help and the help of time, and do not carry out their purpose readily and blamelessly in every respect. So they say what they ought never to have said. For what could we say (and how great are we?) to God the Father, who had but once to will it, and all things came to be through the Son, the Word?

Certainly, of him who is of the seed of David according to the flesh (Romans 1:3), of Abraham, and of the root of Jesse (Isaiah 11:10), it has been proclaimed, as was said just now: “For what has been begotten in her is from the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 1:20); so that from this too it may be agreed that the sanctifying Spirit was fellow-worker with the Creator who works good. That is why it is written again: “Jesus was led in the Spirit into the wilderness” (Luke 4:1); for the guiding Spirit was with him, as God with God, and as one who holds all things together and is present everywhere, with him on whom all things are founded, who is in all things and fills all things. Otherwise, by their reasoning and their way of arguing, neither would the Father be creator or raiser of the dead. For all things came to be through the Son (John 1:3), without toil; for toil is a passion, and passion is a road to corruption.

We say these things without denying that the Master took flesh, without sin, from the nature of Adam, that is, from the Virgin, in other words from our own nature. Rather, we even confirm it by saying that from …

choices.issue: Garbled draft, sentence split across paragraphs, wrong references
choices.choice: 2026-11-11 (claude-sumfix2-e-u17): retranslated. The old English opened with 'Whether it is the Son or the Spirit', made ἐνηργήμεθα active ('nor have we acted'), wrote 'whoever wishes, does not even [create] essence', read ὀλιγωροῦντες as 'stingy', the heretics' saying as 'the one who created the dead, raises the dying alone', and ἀρχιτέκτονος ἀρχιτέκτων as 'an architect of architects'. It broke the sentence 'and since from the beginning ... named together' across two paragraphs, read προελέχθη as 'foreordained', παρενεθυμήθησαν as 'used as an exhortation', turned 'the Father is co-maker by his good pleasure' into 'the Father is a companion to the Son by the will of the Creator', garbled the whole 'they would not have brought ... into comparison' sentence, read ἀπόνως as 'alone', and turned 'neither would the Father be creator' into 'neither by their word ... does the Father raise the dead'. References: (Ezekiel 36:26) -> (Ezekiel 36:26-27), as the reader report says; (Luke 1:35) -> (Matthew 1:20), the words actually quoted; (Matt 4:1) -> (Luke 4:1), whose wording ἤγετο ... ἐν πνεύματι Didymus quotes; (Rom 1:3) -> (Romans 1:3); (Ephesians 2:4), (Job 33:4), (Isaiah 11:10), (John 1:3) added. Bracket '[create]' removed.

choices.english: …Son or the Spirit.
choices.why: The section opens mid-sentence; the previous section ends 'then unlike in no respect will be the …'. Only the words this section holds are translated.

choices.english: who is rich in mercy (Ephesians 2:4)
choices.why: Paul's phrase for God, cited by its wording.

choices.english: nor would we have been worked upon in two ways, and unequally
choices.why: Perfect passive: we are the ones acted upon, not actors.

choices.term: ἄψυχον δημιουργεῖ, ὁ δ' ἂν θέλοι
choices.english: he fashions whatever lifeless thing he may wish
choices.why: ἄψυχον is the thing made; no bracket needed.

choices.english: “breath of the Almighty” (Job 33:4)
choices.why: The words of Job 33:4, quoted earlier in this chapter.

choices.term: οὐχ ἁπλῶς πνεῦμα εἶναι, ἀλλ' ἑαυτοῦ κυρίως
choices.english: that this is not simply a spirit but properly his own
choices.why: Points to 'my Spirit' at the end of the quotation.

choices.english: the arts of outsiders
choices.why: Secular, pagan learning; here the craftsmen's analogy that follows.

choices.term: νεκροὺς ὁ δημιουργήσας, τοὺς νεκρουμένους ἐγείρει μόνος
choices.english: “The dead, those who are put to death, are raised only by him who created them.
choices.why: νεκροὺς and τοὺς νεκρουμένους are the object of ἐγείρει; ὁ δημιουργήσας ... μόνος is the subject. The quotation marks run to the end of the opponents' argument (Eve), since φησίν recurs inside it.

choices.english: a master builder repairs a master builder’s work
choices.why: Genitive of the work; διορθώσαιτο is understood from the first clause.

choices.english: by the common principle of nature
choices.why: λόγος here is the principle or account of the shared nature, not a spoken word.

choices.term: ἀχωρίστως εἶχεν τῇ θεότητι καὶ τῇ ἐνεργείᾳ
choices.english: was inseparable from him in Godhead and in working
choices.why: ἔχω with an adverb = 'be in a state'; 'from him' (God) is plain English from συμπαρῆν.

choices.term: εἰ μὴ οὖν ἑτέρως μὲν ταῖς γραφαῖς, ἑτέρως δὲ αὐτοῖς ἐκείνοις ἐδόκει
choices.english: If, then, it had not seemed one thing to the Scriptures and another to these men
choices.why: Contrary-to-fact condition; the two apodoses (πρῶτον ... δεύτερον) follow with ἄν.

choices.english: they would ... have taken to heart
choices.why: The context needs a positive verb; see problems.

choices.english: the one who uttered these oracles
choices.why: χράω, 'deliver an oracle': God, the author of the Scriptures.

choices.term: τοῦ υἱοῦ κτίσαντος συμποιητὴς ὁ πατήρ ἐστιν τῇ εὐδοκήσει
choices.english: the Father is co-maker by his good pleasure when the Son creates
choices.why: Genitive absolute; the old English made 'the Creator' a third party.

choices.term: καὶ οὐκ ... ἤγαγον ... λέγοντες, ἅπερ μήποτ' ἔφασαν
choices.english: And they would not have dragged the things of the blessed Trinity ... into comparison with things unlike it ... So they say what they ought never to have said.
choices.why: ἄν carries over from ἐλογίσαντο ἄν; δημιουργοὺς λόγων τε καὶ ὑλῶν ἐπισκευῆς is in apposition to ἡμᾶς (we are the craftsmen the opponents compare with God). The long period is split into English sentences.

choices.term: τί γὰρ ἢ ὡς πηλίκοι εἴποιμεν
choices.english: For what could we say (and how great are we?)
choices.why: ὡς πηλίκοι, 'as how great', is a hedge of human smallness before God.

choices.term: ἐκ σπέρματος ∆αυὶδ καὶ Ἀβραὰμ καὶ ἐκ ῥίζης Ἰεσσαὶ κατὰ σάρκα
choices.english: of the seed of David according to the flesh (Romans 1:3), of Abraham, and of the root of Jesse (Isaiah 11:10)
choices.why: Romans 1:3 has 'seed of David according to the flesh'; Isaiah 11:10 'root of Jesse'. 'Of Abraham' (Matthew 1:1) is left uncited to avoid a third parenthesis in one clause.

choices.english: the guiding Spirit
choices.why: The phrase of Greek Psalm 50:14 (English 51:12); listed as a possible allusion.

choices.term: ἐπεὶ μή γε ... οὔτε ὁ πατὴρ δημιουργὸς ἢ νεκροὺς ἐγείρων
choices.english: Otherwise, by their reasoning ... neither would the Father be creator or raiser of the dead
choices.why: Reductio: if only the one who made can raise, and all things were made through the Son, the Father would be neither.

choices.term: ὅ ἐστιν ἐκ τῆς παρθένου, ἢ τῆς ἡμετέρας
choices.english: that is, from the Virgin, in other words from our own nature
choices.why: ἢ here explains rather than offers an alternative: Adam's nature is ours.

choices.english: by saying that from …
choices.why: The section ends on ἐκ; the next section holds the rest of the phrase. Only the word held here is translated, ending with '…'.

choices.english: page debris
choices.why: 71 and 72 are printed page numbers, skipped; ἀφε λῶ is one word split across a printed line.
